lede: Several forces pulling one body can always be replaced by a single force that would do exactly the same job. That single force is the resultant, and finding it is the same two-column arithmetic every time: total across, total up.
can: Find the resultant of two or more forces given in i and j form
Resolve forces given at angles and total the two directions
Work out the magnitude and the direction of a resultant

md: The resultant is the single force with the same effect as the whole set. It has a size and a direction, so an answer is finished only when both are given, or when it is written in $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ form. Forces pulling different ways never simply add up: their directions decide the total.

stem: Two forces of 11 N and 6 N act at a point. How big can their resultant be?

steps.decision: Pulling together, the whole of each counts: the largest the resultant can be.
Pulling against each other, the smaller cancels part of the larger: the smallest it can be.
Any other direction gives a size between those two.

prompt: Forces of 35 N and 12 N act at a point in different directions. Which could be the size of their resultant?
explain: In different directions the resultant lies between the difference, $35 - 12 = 23$ N, and the sum, $47$ N, as steps 1 and 2 of See it showed; 47 N needs both to point the same way, so 37 N is the only one possible.

twin.prompt: Forces of 20 N and 9 N act at a point in different directions. Which could be the size of their resultant?
twin.explain: Between the difference, 11 N, and the sum, 29 N; the sum itself needs both to point the same way.

optionNotes.why: 29 N is their sum, which needs both forces to point the same way; in different directions the resultant is less.
That is more than their sum, 29 N, and no pair of 20 N and 9 N can make more than that.
47 N is their sum, which needs both forces to point the same way; in different directions part of each works against the other.
That is more than their sum, 47 N, and no pair of 35 N and 12 N can make more than that.

text: In i and j: total each column

md: When the forces are given in components the work is arithmetic: total the $\mathbf{i}$ parts, total the $\mathbf{j}$ parts, and keep the two columns apart. Watch the negatives: adding $-5$ takes five away, and subtracting a force instead of adding it is a slip the reports have seen here.

stem: Find the resultant of $(5\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ N, $(-8\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j})$ N and $(6\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N.

steps.decision: Total the i column on its own, each number with its sign.
Then the j column, separately: nothing crosses between them.
The two totals side by side are the resultant in i and j form.

prompt: Two forces are $(10\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-7\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})$ N. What is their resultant?
explain: Column by column, as See it did: $10 - 7 = 3$ across and $-2 + 6 = 4$ up, so the resultant is $3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$ N. Subtracting the second force instead of adding it is the slip to avoid.

twin.prompt: Two forces are $(9\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-5\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})$ N. What is their resultant?
twin.answer: 4i - 2j | 4i-2j | 4i − 2j | 4i - 2j N | 4i-2j N | -2j + 4i | R = 4i - 2j | (4i - 2j) N | (4i - 2j) | 4i - 2j newtons | 4 i - 2 j

caption: Each force split before anything is added.

md: Forces given at angles are resolved before they are combined. Take to the right and upwards as positive, resolve every force into those two directions, then total each direction. A force pointing left or down counts negative in its total.

stem: Three forces pull a point: 26 N to the right, 15 N at 40° above the horizontal to the right, and 8 N to the left. Total each direction.

steps.decision: Right positive: the 8 N force points left, so it is subtracted.
The two horizontal forces have no upward part.

prompt: A force of 20 N acts horizontally to the right and a force of 6 N acts horizontally to the left. What is the total component to the right, in newtons?
explain: The second force points the other way, so it is subtracted, as the 8 N force was in step 1 of See it: $20 - 6 = 14$ N.

twin.prompt: A force of 17 N acts horizontally to the right and a force of 23 N acts horizontally to the left. What is the total component to the right, in newtons?
twin.explain: $17 - 23 = -6$ N: the total is negative because the larger force points left.

caption: The two totals are the legs; the resultant is the longest side.

md: The across total and the up total are at right angles, so they are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle and the resultant is its longest side. That makes the magnitude $\sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$, on the Unit 2 formula sheet as the magnitude of $x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$.
Keep the totals unrounded in the calculator until the last line. Rounding a total before squaring it can move the second decimal place of the magnitude, and the mark for the value goes with it.

stem: The forces on a body total 16 N across and 12 N up. Find the magnitude of the resultant.

steps.decision: The two totals are the shorter sides; the resultant is the longest.
Square, add, then take the square root: the root is the step most often left off.

title: A-Level Maths: R1-12 Forces: Finding the Magnitude and Direction of a Resultant Force
why: The two totals, then Pythagoras, then the angle, worked at a slower pace. Watch the diagram being drawn before either calculation starts.

prompt: The forces on a body have a total component of 8 N to the right and 6 N upwards. What is the magnitude of the resultant, in newtons?
explain: The two totals are perpendicular, so Pythagoras applies, as in See it: $\sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ N. Adding them, 14 N, treats them as pulling the same way.

caption: The angle is measured from the line the question names.

md: In the same triangle the up total is opposite the angle with the horizontal and the across total is beside it, so $\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{Y}{X}$: the angle with the horizontal, the line these questions almost always name.
Name the line in the answer, as in '28.07° above the horizontal'. A resultant pointing down or to the left still takes the inverse tangent of the two sizes; the sketch says which way it points.

title: Why the fraction goes that way up
md: Tangent is opposite over adjacent. Measuring from the horizontal makes the up total the opposite side and the across total the adjacent one, so the up total goes on top.

stem: A resultant has totals of 15 N across and 8 N up. Find the angle it makes with the horizontal.

steps.decision: The up total is opposite the angle, so it goes on top.
Name the line it is measured from.
The fraction turned over gives the angle with the vertical, a different answer.

prompt: A resultant has a total component of $X$ to the right and $Y$ upwards. Which expression gives the angle it makes with the horizontal?
explain: The up total is opposite the angle with the horizontal and the across total beside it, as in step 1 of See it, so the up total goes on top. Turning the fraction over gives the angle with the vertical.

twin.prompt: A resultant has a total component of $X$ to the right and $Y$ upwards. Which expression gives the angle it makes with the vertical?
twin.explain: Measured from the vertical, the across total is opposite the angle, so it goes on top.

optionNotes.why: That is the angle with the horizontal; measured from the vertical, the across total is opposite the angle and goes on top.
Cosine compares a side with the longest side, the resultant; the two totals compared with each other give a tangent.
That is the fraction turned over, which gives the angle with the vertical rather than the horizontal.
Sine compares a side with the longest side, the resultant; the two totals compared with each other give a tangent.

md: **The missing force** (2023). The resultant is given and one force is not: take the forces you know away from the resultant, column by column. **Both parts at once** (every year): a part may ask for the resultant in $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ and then its magnitude and direction, each using the one before.
**An angle turned into i and j**: a force given by its size and angle is written in components first, then added in columns.

stem: $(6\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})$ N is the resultant of $(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$ N, $(-\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{c}$. Find $\mathbf{c}$.

steps.decision: The three forces add to R, so c is what is left once a and b are taken away.
Column by column, each sign reversed as it is taken away.
Check: a + b + c gives R back.

prompt: The resultant of $(3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N, $(-\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ N and a third force $\mathbf{c}$ is $(5\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})$ N. What is $\mathbf{c}$?
explain: Take the known forces from the resultant, as in See it: across $5 - 3 + 1 = 3$, up $1 - 2 - 4 = -5$, so $\mathbf{c} = 3\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j}$ N. Adding them all would give the resultant of four forces.

twin.prompt: The resultant of $(3\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})$ N, $(2\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})$ N and a third force $\mathbf{c}$ is $(9\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})$ N. What is $\mathbf{c}$?
twin.answer: 4i + 4j | 4i+4j | 4j + 4i | 4i + 4j N | 4i+4j N | c = 4i + 4j | (4i + 4j) N | (4i + 4j) | 4i + 4j newtons | 4 i + 4 j

text: An unknown part from the magnitude

md: **A magnitude given** (2021). The size is given and one part is unknown: square both parts, add, and set the total equal to the size squared. The equation gives two roots; the question's picture or wording says which sign to keep.

stem: A resultant force $(x\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j})$ N has a magnitude of 10 N. Find $x$.

steps.decision: The magnitude squared is the sum of the two parts squared.
Take the known part's square away.
Both roots fit the size; keep the one the question asks for.

prompt: A resultant force $(x\mathbf{i} + 40\mathbf{j})$ N has a magnitude of 41 N. What is the positive value of $x$?

twin.prompt: A resultant force $(x\mathbf{i} + 15\mathbf{j})$ N has a magnitude of 17 N. What is the positive value of $x$?

md:
Add forces in i and j by totalling the two columns, negatives included.
Resolve forces at angles and total the across and up directions.
Find the magnitude from the two totals with Pythagoras.
Find the direction with an inverse tangent, from the line the question names.
Find a missing force, or an unknown part from a given magnitude.

Question 1 or 2 gives forces in i and j, or at angles, and asks for the resultant, then its magnitude for 2 to 4 marks and its direction for 2. The first mark is for the two totals written down; the last is for the angle to 2 decimal places, measured from the line the question names. Stuck? Write the across total and the up total on separate lines before anything else.
